prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B034 to B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. In round 1 I said I would move B028 up if the condensed-matter colleagues could agree on a defensible trio. The chair's summary shows that four members, working independently, named exactly this slate. What decided it for me is the scientific question I try to ask of every candidate: did nature tell us something we did not expect, and was it checked by others? Spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry gives a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge channels in an insulator with no magnetic field. That is a new state of matter, predicted in a minimal model (Kane and Mele), and then seen in HgTe wells (Molenkamp, 2007) and later in many other materials by many groups. I know this kind of theory-plus-decisive-experiment chain well from my own work, and the reproduction here is wider than for any other shortlisted candidate. On the question of distinctness from 2016: that prize honoured topological phase transitions and the quantised Hall conductance in model and magnetic-field systems. B028 is about symmetry-protected band topology in ordinary non-magnetic materials, which is a different mechanism and a different set of experiments. The citation should say that in plain words and should be written narrowly enough (the prediction and the first observation of the quantum spin Hall state) that the omission of the 3D strand and of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is not a misstatement of history.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and I have not made it go away. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that made Molenkamp's experiment possible, and the 3D strand (Fu, Kane and Mele; Moore and Balents; Roy; Hasan's ARPES) stays outside a trio. The HgTe edge conductance fell short of perfect quantisation, so a sceptic can say the experimental half is thin. Practical applications are modest. If the committee judges the 2016 prize to have already reached this ground, B028 is weaker than I now argue. I also remain a non-specialist in condensed matter and rely on Eriksson, Mehlig, Johansson and Olsson for the priority history; I cannot verify the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu-Moore-Balents-Roy claims independently.

responses.point: Kroll asks me, as a B034 supporter, to name a concrete finding obtained with lattice clocks that nature did not allow us to guess, and he says the new observables are prospects and not results.
responses.response: I have tried to answer honestly and I cannot give you a finding that is as strong as I wanted. The millimetre-scale redshift measurement and the many-body, spin-exchange and Fermi-degenerate effects seen in the lattice are real results, and I like them. But they confirm what theory expected and are not a surprise from nature. The magic-wavelength condition worked as predicted. The achievement is a method and a record in precision, with very clean credit, and I still think it is strong. But your question showed me that I was partly arguing from the elegance of the polarizability calculation, which is exactly the bias I flagged in round 1. I therefore move B034 to an alternative and I would not object if the committee picked it later, once the redefinition of the second has happened or the clocks have produced a new physical result.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and says openly that a slate with Hasan for the 3D case would be at least as defensible, and that the HgTe edge conductance was imperfectly quantised.
responses.response: I agree with your account of the strength of the Z2 idea and I take your caveat seriously. On Hasan, my judgement is that the citation can honestly be limited to the quantum spin Hall prediction and its first observation, and that the trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp matches that wording exactly. Replacing Mele or Molenkamp with Hasan would make the prize a 'topological insulators as a class' prize and would then raise the Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy question, which a three-name limit cannot answer. On the imperfect quantisation: the edge conductance was near the predicted value in the shortest samples and was reproduced later in other structures, which I count as sufficient confirmation. I would keep your narrow wording.

responses.point: Danielsson asks what a topological-insulator prize adds that 2016 did not, and says 'rigorously analysable' is not itself a Nobel criterion.
responses.response: I agree that analysability is not the criterion, and I do not rely on it. My answer is that nature supplied the content: a bulk insulator with conducting edge states protected by time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling, with no magnetic field, seen first in HgTe and then in other materials. The 2016 citation was about topological phase transitions and Hall-type quantisation, and this is a different class of system and a different mechanism. As for your two-part configuration, I understand why you want to honour two distinct discoveries, but I do not find the IceCube credit defensible with one name, and the Chair's own answer (that Halzen conceived the concept) concerns leadership more than the discovery. You have said you would not oppose B028 if B005 falls, and I think B028 alone is the cleaner outcome.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B028 first, accepts that the trio is defensible but not unique, and treats the Z2 classification as the unifying step that connects the HgTe and Bi-based surface-state experiments.
responses.response: In round 1 I answered you that I would move B028 up if the condensed-matter members could settle on a trio. You and three others did that, so I am doing it. I find your argument that the Z2 classification unifies the 2D and 3D cases scientifically persuasive, but it argues for a citation worded around the Z2 idea and the first observation, not for adding a fourth name. As a theorist you also know that band-structure calculations and spectra agree well in these materials, which is the sort of theory and measurement agreement I trust. I would ask that the background text record the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang prediction, and the 3D work, in explicit terms.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B046 with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer, would not wait for the pairing mechanism, but treats B028 as the strongest fallback and shares the attribution doubts about the 2D and 3D strands.
responses.response: I respect the B046 case and I have not forgotten that all eight of us ranked it. My view is that the pairing mechanism is a secondary issue, as your cuprate comparison shows. The real reasons I place it behind B028 are the eight-year age of the discovery and the open credit questions for Andrei, Cao and Fatemi, which you describe yourself. The B028 credit problem is of the same kind but the field has had fifteen years of independent confirmation, so I find its facts more settled. I keep B046 as my second alternative because it is the candidate that I expect the committee will need to return to, and I would back it if the B028 trio proved indefensible.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the quantum spin Hall prediction plus first observation as sufficiently distinct from the 2016 topological-phase prize; I rely on my colleagues in condensed matter for this.

Whether the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang prediction and the Hasan and Fu-Moore-Balents-Roy work give claims that make a three-name B028 prize unsafe; I cannot verify the priority history from what I have.
Whether my change away from B034 is an over-correction caused by my worry about favouring my own field, since I still regard the lattice-clock case as strong and cleanly credited.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene is ready now; I defer to the condensed-matter members on the pairing mechanism and on how to weigh Andrei's earlier STM work.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with attosecond groups at Lund and ETH. I work in the same atomic, molecular and optical community as the clock and ultracold-atom candidates (B034, B011), and B034 is close to my own field, which is one reason I treated my earlier preference with caution. I have no collaboration with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Katori, Ye or any other credited name that I know of from my profile. I report no new conflict and I do not think any of these requires recusal on B028, but I leave the chair to decide on B034 and B011.
